extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners and patent practitioners (applicants and attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for evaluating compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112 (written description, enablement, means-plus-function, and best mode), including examination procedure, burdens of proof, and key legal factors and examples. Applies to assessing whether a specification discloses and enables the full scope of claimed subject matter (including computer-implemented and biological inventions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description must demonstrate possession
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The description may use words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas; possession can be shown by reduction to practice, disclosure that the invention was "ready for patenting," or distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficient to show possession. Compliance is fact-based and varies with the nature of the invention (citations: Moba; Vas-Cath; Pfaff; Eli Lilly; Amgen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement: make and use without undue experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: To satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (enablement), the specification must teach those skilled in the art how to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without "undue experimentation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing undue experimentation, weigh the Wands factors: (1) breadth of the claims; (2) nature of the invention; (3) state of the prior art; (4) level of ordinary skill; (5) level of predictability in the art; (6) amount of direction provided by the inventor; (7) existence of working examples; and (8) quantity of experimentation needed. Examination requires a reasonable basis for questioning enablement; once shown, applicant must rebut with factual demonstration (cites: In re Wands; In re Wright; In re Brown; In re Ghiron; In re Doyle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of claims must be commensurate with enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of the claims must be less than or equal to the scope of the enablement provided by the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad, functional claim language (not invoking 112(f)) is construed broadly to cover any embodiment performing the function; examiner must ensure the specification enables the full claim scope. Examples: Sitrick (video games vs. movies) and MagSil (resistive-change magnitude) show patentees choosing broad claim language at risk of invalidity if full scope isn't enabled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot rely on ordinary skill to supply novel information
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification need not teach what is well known in the art, but the applicant cannot rely on the knowledge of one skilled in the art to supply information required to enable the novel aspect of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The novel aspects of an invention must be enabled in the specification itself; omission of specific starting materials or conditions that are necessary to carry out the invention can render it non-enabled (cites: ALZA; Auto. Technologies; Genentech).

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-(or step-)plus-function limitations require corresponding structure/materials/acts
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim includes a means- (or step-) plus-function limitation under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (or pre-AIA sixth paragraph), the specification must disclose sufficient corresponding structure, materials, or acts that perform the entire claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no sufficient corresponding structure is disclosed, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or written description may be required; and a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA second paragraph) must be made in addition to a written description rejection (cites: In re Donaldson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode: subjective knowledge and objective disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination of best mode requires (1) a subjective inquiry into whether the inventor actually knew of a best mode at filing, and (2) an objective inquiry into whether that best mode was disclosed in sufficient detail to allow one skilled in the art to practice it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The purpose is to prevent inventors from concealing preferred embodiments. Only evidence of concealment (accidental or intentional) is considered; to sustain a best mode rejection, evidence must show the disclosure quality is so poor as to effectively result in concealment. For software as best mode, disclosure of functions normally suffices—flowcharts or source code listings are not required (cites: In re Gay; Spectra-Physics; In re Sherwood; Fonar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional-only descriptions may fail written description
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention described solely in terms of a method of making and/or its function may lack written descriptive support where there is no described or art-recognized correlation between the disclosed function and the structure(s) responsible for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include protein/amino-acid/genetic claims where sequence/function correlation is required; merely rendering a claimed invention obvious does not necessarily satisfy written description (cites: In re Bell; In re Deuel; Eli Lilly; Fonar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Original claims: presumption of adequate written description but still fact-specific
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a presumption that an adequate written description exists when the application is filed, but original claims may still lack adequate written description if essential or critical features are not described with sufficient particularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner has initial burden to present reasons why skilled artisans would not recognize the claim in the disclosure. Even originally-filed claims must be examined to ensure all limitations, especially non-conventional ones, are adequately supported (cites: In re Wertheim; Vas-Cath; cases like Gentry Gallery, Tronzo).

rubrics_metrics.name: New or amended claims must be supported by originally-filed disclosure (no new matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: New or amended claims that introduce elements or limitations not supported by the as-filed disclosure violate the written description requirement and the prohibition against adding new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support may be express, implicit, or inherent; correcting obvious errors is permissible when an ordinary artisan would recognize the error and correction. For sequence corrections and biological deposits, post-filing deposits may support corrections only if accompanied by required statements (cites: 35 U.S.C. 132/251; In re Rasmussen; In re Benno; Cubist v. Hospira; 37 CFR 1.801/1.804).

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential or critical features disclosed as essential cannot be omitted from claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification describes a limitation as essential or critical to the invention, omission of that limitation in a claim may render the claim noncompliant with the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that omit matter disclosed as essential may also be subject to enablement or 112(b)/second paragraph rejections. Cases: Gentry Gallery, In re Sus, Tronzo, and others illustrating that the disclosure can 'make crystal clear' a narrow understanding of a term that cannot be broadened (citations in text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposit of biological materials may aid written description but is not a substitute
rubrics_metrics.description: A deposit made under 37 CFR 1.801 et seq. may satisfy written description for claimed biological materials where appropriate, but such a deposit is not a substitute for a complete written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification should include as much information about the deposited material as possible to aid examiner comparison with prior art and to permit verification; post-filing deposits can support sequence corrections only with required statements (cites: Enzo Biochem; 54 Fed. Reg. 34,864; In re Lundak).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner must establish reasonable basis before enablement rejection; applicant must rebut
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO personnel must establish on the record a reasonable basis for questioning the adequacy of the disclosure to enable a person of ordinary skill to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once the examiner has advanced a reasonable basis, the burden shifts to the applicant to rebut and factually demonstrate the disclosure is sufficient. Examiners should provide reasons for questioning enablement and follow with thorough review of prior art and other statutory requirements before completing an Office action (cites: In re Brown; In re Ghiron; In re Doyle; MPEP §§ 2164 et seq.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional claim language without invoking 112(f) broadens claim scope and raises enablement/written_description concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim is not limited to any particular structure for a recited function and does not invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f), the claim language is typically construed broadly to cover any and all embodiments performing that function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because such claims encompass potentially all devices/structures that perform the function, examiners must be concerned whether the disclosure sufficiently enables the full scope; applicants presenting broad claim language must ensure their specification fully enables across that scope (cites: In re Swinehart; AK Steel v. Sollac; In re Moore).

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description and enablement are separate requirements with distinct objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: The written description requirement (demonstrating possession and informing the public of what is claimed) is separate and distinct from the enablement requirement (teaching how to make and use without undue experimentation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both are minimum requirements under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (first paragraph); failure to satisfy either can result in rejection or invalidity. Examiners should assess both independently (cites: Ariad; Vas-Cath; Univ. of Rochester v. G.D. Searle).
